meta.title: Who really said "We are all broken. That's how the light gets in"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Rumi: Quote Investigator traces this line to a blend of Hemingway's 1929 novel and Leonard Cohen's 1992 song Anthem. It surfaced online in 2013.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We are all broken. That's how the light gets in'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Rumi and not Hemingway. Half of it is Leonard Cohen's Anthem (1992); the rest is a rewrite of A Farewell to Arms. The composite dates from 2013.

answer.label: Not Rumi — a Hemingway/Cohen mash-up
answer.authorDates: Origin unidentified · a composite of Hemingway (1929) and Cohen (1992) · neither man wrote this sentence
answer.sourceLine: The closing clause belongs to Leonard Cohen, from “Anthem” on his 1992 album The Future; the opening echoes Hemingway’s A Farewell to Arms (1929), whose actual sentence reads “The world breaks everyone and afterward many are strong at the broken places.” Quote Investigator ↗ found no evidence that anyone — Hemingway, Cohen or Rumi — wrote the combined sentence; the earliest instance it documents is a tweet of 8 June 2013 crediting Hemingway.

source.excerpt: The world breaks everyone and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills.
trail: 1841 — the oldest ancestor Quote Investigator identifies ↗ is Ralph Waldo Emerson’s essay “Compensation,” whose text reads “There is a crack in every thing God has made” (full essay on Wikisource ↗). In context it is a warning, not a comfort.

1929 — Hemingway’s A Farewell to Arms, ch. 34: “The world breaks everyone and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills” (sourced on Wikiquote ↗). The novel was serialized in Scribner’s Magazine from May to October 1929 and published in book form that September ↗.
1992 — Leonard Cohen’s “Anthem,” on The Future ↗, gives the closing clause its exact wording.
2013–2016 — the composite surfaces: Quote Investigator’s earliest instance ↗ is a tweet of 8 June 2013 signed with Hemingway’s name, and it reaches print by 8 May 2016 in the Lansing State Journal.
source.excerptNote: This is the closest real sentence by any of the three named authors — and it is not consoling. Hemingway offers no light through the break, only survival for some and death for the rest. The quotable version reverses the mood, which is a good sign that it was assembled by someone else.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this sentence: it has no identified author and no first publication — the earliest instance documented is an anonymous 2013 tweet. For the parts, the picture differs: Hemingway’s A Farewell to Arms, first published in 1929, is in the public domain in the United States, while Leonard Cohen’s “Anthem” (1992) is firmly in copyright and should not be reproduced as lyrics.

author.name: Leonard Cohen
author.kicker: The man behind the half that is real
author.heading: Whose words actually survive in this line
author.bio: Leonard Cohen was a novelist and poet before he was a recording artist, and he worked slowly: Anthem, the song on his 1992 album The Future whose refrain pairs a crack in everything with the light that comes through it, took him about a decade to finish. That refrain is the one genuinely authored piece of this internet sentence — the second half. The first half, “We are all broken”, is not his, and the two-part line as it circulates appears nowhere in his work.

misattribution.heading: Three famous names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This sentence is a magnet: it has been hung on a novelist, a songwriter and a 13th-century Persian poet, and the research says none of them wrote it in this form.

items.why: The dominant credit online, and the one Quote Investigator ↗ tested: it concludes the quotation was not crafted by Hemingway and finds nothing earlier than a tweet of 8 June 2013 carrying his name. Goodreads ↗ still lists it under Hemingway — while tagging it misattributed-ernest-hemingway.

Rumi gets pulled in through Coleman Barks’s 1995 version of “Childhood Friends,” which ends by telling the reader to keep looking at the bandaged place because that is where the light enters — a different image, in a modern English rendering. Quote Investigator files this investigation under Rumi ↗ for exactly that reason, and identifies no Rumi text as the source of the sentence.

“That’s how the light gets in” really is Cohen’s, from “Anthem” on the 1992 album The Future ↗. The first half is not: his refrain is about a crack in everything, not about all of us being broken. Goodreads tags the composite misattributed-leonard-cohen as well.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗: the quotation was not crafted by Hemingway, its exact genesis is uncertain, and Hemingway’s 1929 statement plus Cohen’s 1992 lyric both strongly influenced how the expression — and its ascription — evolved.

context.heading: How a consolation was assembled out of two other people’s sentences
lead: Every part of this line has a real ancestor, and none of them says what the line says. Ralph Waldo Emerson’s essay “Compensation” carries the sentence “There is a crack in every thing God has made” — a warning that nothing in nature comes free, not a comfort. Hemingway’s version in A Farewell to Arms is bleaker still: the world breaks everyone, some are stronger afterwards, and the ones who will not break are killed. Leonard Cohen’s “Anthem” supplied the consoling turn — the crack as the way in for light — and that is the half that survives verbatim.

What the internet did was cut the grimness off Hemingway’s clause, weld it to Cohen’s, and hand the result to whichever famous name suited the reader: Hemingway first, from 2013, and Rumi later, by way of a Coleman Barks rendering about a bandaged place that light enters. The mash-up is more quotable than any of its sources, which is exactly why it spread and why none of its supposed authors ever wrote it.
context.detailsSummary: The chain of precursors Quote Investigator documents
detailsBody: 1841 — Emerson’s “Compensation”: “There is a crack in every thing God has made.” 1860 — Benjamin Blood’s Optimism: The Lesson of Ages joins Emerson’s crack to light coming through it. 1929 — Hemingway’s broken places. 1992 — Cohen’s “Anthem.” 1995 — Coleman Barks’s version of Rumi’s “Childhood Friends,” which ends on a bandaged place where light enters. All five are documented on Quote Investigator ↗.

By 8 May 2016 the composite had made it off social media and into print: Quote Investigator cites it that day in the Lansing State Journal, printed as a Lansing Catholic High School student’s favourite quotation.
context.pull: Hemingway said the world breaks you and kills the unbreakable. That is not a fridge magnet, so someone built one.
